subject: Fitting a Multidimensional IRT Model in Stan

messages.author: f94f7db4d63c49bd
messages.subject: Fitting a Multidimensional IRT Model in Stan
parts:
Hi Everyone,

I wrote two blog posts about fitting IRT models in Stan. I have provided code that I hope might be of benefit to people who are fitting similar models in Stan. Here are the links

Multidimensional IRT with plots rendered using the rbokeh package: http://rfarouni.github.io/code/2015/04/22/mirt/

2PL unidimensional IRT model with results of fit exported to ShinyStan: http://rfarouni.github.io/code/2015/03/20/irt/

I apologize for an errors you might in the posts. Feedback is very welcome.

Thanks,
Rick Farouni

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Fitting a Multidimensional IRT Model in Stan
parts:
Thanks for sharing! I love these knitr docs that include
everything for a model from simulation to fit. It's the format
I'd like to adopt for all of our examples (at least those done
in R --- IPython Notebooks would do the same work).

Identification's a tricky business. Presumably Doug Rivers
was talking about MLE identification in his 2003 paper.
I'm not sure how your parameterization in terms of a product
minus a sum is identifiable --- it always hurts my head to
think about these.

We'd have made your life a lot easier if we had a lower-triangular
data type or even general ragged matrices!

That knitr-HTML-rendered LaTeX could use some work in spacing,
like between probablity terms in multiplications.

I didn't understand the hex plot. Why are there hexagons and
why are they all touching?

The print output's still too much to scan in a presentation, but
it's nice to see it so users know what to do if they follow your example.
I'm always torn about that, because a visualization of the means (and
perhaps uncertainties) would be easier to scan --- maybe even scatterplots
of the two alpha components.

The person order vs. number of correct responses is hard to
understand --- wouldn't a histogram have been easier?

- Bob

Probably, a two dimensional histogram could have been as effective, but I couldn't resist the colorful display.  I have only started using them, but  I guess that the hexagons are touching for the same reason rectangles in a histogram abut each other.

The print output's still too much to scan in a presentation, but
it's nice to see it so users know what to do if they follow your example.
I'm always torn about that, because a visualization of the means (and
perhaps uncertainties) would be easier to scan --- maybe even scatterplots
of the two alpha components.
I agree. A very good point.

The person order vs. number of correct responses is hard to
understand --- wouldn't a histogram have been easier?

I used this plot because  a histogram won't show any deviations from, or the variability of, the linear trend we expect to see. Namely, the higher the latent ability on one dimension, the higher the proportion of correct responses.

- Bob

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Fitting a Multidimensional IRT Model in Stan
parts:
The idea is that hexagonal tilings don’t introduce a visual
bias to the axes like a square tiling does (in a square tiling
diagonal moves are awkward and so the eye tends to follow
horizontal and vertical lines).  In practice that’s way more
relevant to tabletop games (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hex_map)
and I’ve never found it particularly compelling as a
visualization argument.  If the appearance of the plot is that 
sensitive to the tiling then make the tiles smaller, and if you
can’t make them any smaller than you don’t really have enough
data yield a reasonable histogram estimator of the density.
